headline: Twelve repeated class strings is the case where a cached merger is nearly free, so what remains visible is whether variant selection happens in the compiler or on every render.

microbench.why: With only about twelve distinct class strings, `cnfast` (0.689 ms/1k) and `tailwind-merge` (0.886) are essentially cache lookups, and `next-yak-9.7` (0.601) compiles the variant into `$prop` class toggles that fold to a string concatenation. `panda` at 1.57 ms/1k merges the conditional objects on every render, 1.03 ms of component self-time and 29.2 ms inside its own package, while `bamboo` at 0.719 ships the same `css()` API and cannot express that shape at all: its compiler rejects a conditional inside one call, forcing five static calls joined by `cx()` that compile to class-string literals. `panda`'s own precompiled `cva` recipe confirms the mechanism from inside the same library at 0.789 ms/1k. Spreads here reach 19%, so read the clusters and not the order.

autocannon.why: `next-yak-9.7` serves 1,540 req/s and `vanilla` 1,390. `bamboo` at 980 and `panda`'s recipe at 879 pay in class-attribute bytes, and `panda`'s `css()` build at 510 pays in per-request merging on top. `emotion` (339) and `styled-components` (516) re-derive the variant's class on every request rather than once per variant.

attribution.why: Where the class string is decided at build time the render is react-dom and little else: `next-yak-9.7` 0.600 ms with a 0.259 ms library slice, `next-yak-css-9.7` 0.666, `stylex-layers` 0.694 with none. `panda` puts 1.03 of its 1.47 ms into component self-time resolving merged objects to atomic classes, and its `cva` recipe halves that to 0.488 from identical CSS. `bamboo`'s 1.74 ms is the odd figure in the case: its library slice is zero and its JS window is only 32.3 ms, but 19.7 ms of the profile is garbage collection, which the wall-clock microbench does not show.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

hydrate.why: The variant button hydrates as pure JS wherever the sheet is a file, 44.8-58.4 ms for the folded, atomic and recipe builds with zero style and zero layout inside the span. `goober` (97.5 ms) and `styled-components` (102 ms) inject and pay 0.20-0.22 ms of recalculation plus a 2.3-3.6 ms layout. Spreads inside the fast cluster reach 45%, so its internal order carries no signal.

inp.why: Toggling the variant re-renders one button, and every lane that decided its class at build time does the toggle as a string swap: 6.9-8.1 ms across all of them, one measurement wide. `panda` at 7.6 ms now sits inside that cluster; `emotion` at 12.3 ms is the only lane where changing a variant costs measurable work, re-hashing the new rule set.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

mount.why: Cold mount is one sheet parse plus first paint, 75.5-79.7 ms for the build-time lanes, `bamboo` at 79.7 among them because its work already happened during the build. `emotion` (106 ms), `styled-components` (93.2) and `goober` (92.8) build the sheet first; `goober`'s 16.6 ms layout against the cluster's 6.1-7.0 shows the browser waiting on it.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation and one layout per lane, so the counts tie and only recalc cost separates them, 0.124-0.228 ms. A variant toggle changes which class an element carries, not how often Chrome has to recalculate a static sheet.

payload.why: The css-prop fold ships 3.39 kB gzipped, below `vanilla`'s 3.79, because five variant rules collapse into numbered classes on one element. `bamboo` ships 6.73 kB and `panda`'s recipe 6.91, while `panda`'s `css()` build adds its resolver for 9.80 kB. The utility lanes carry a scanned sheet whatever the page uses, `cnfast` 16.1 kB and `tailwind-merge` 15.1.

nsweep.why: At 4,000 buttons the class-toggle concatenation holds 2.04 ms and `bamboo`'s literal join 2.43, both linear in n. `panda` reaches 5.49 ms and its recipe 2.68, the same library separated only by whether the variant was resolved during the build. `emotion` (11.3 ms) and `goober` (7.80) scale their hash the same way.
